‘Well, you naughty fellow,’ the old lady exclaimed as he came in, ‘why have you stayed away from me for so long?’

‘My dear Lady Clem, I never get a moment to myself,’ Lord Arthur answered with a smile.

‘I suppose you mean that you spend every day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying fripperies and talking rubbish. I cannot see why people make such a production of getting married. In my day, we would never have dreamt of cooing over each other in public—or in private, for that matter.’

‘I assure you, Lady Clem, I haven’t seen Sybil in twenty-four hours. As far as I can tell, her hatmakers have taken complete possession of her.’

‘Naturally. That is the only reason you visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder why you men never learn. Men have done foolish things for my sake, and look at me now: a wretched rheumatic creature with false hair and a foul temper. Really, without dear Lady Jansen sending me the most scandalous French novels she can find, I don’t know how I would get through the day. Doctors do nothing except collect their fees. They can’t even cure my heartburn.’

‘I’ve brought you something to cure that, Lady Clem,’ Lord Arthur said solemnly. ‘It is a marvellous invention by an American.’

‘I don’t believe I like American inventions, Arthur. In fact, I am certain I don’t. I recently read some American novels, and they were utterly absurd.’

‘But there is nothing absurd about this, Lady Clem. I promise you it works perfectly. You must say you’ll try it.’ Lord Arthur took the little box from his pocket and gave it to her.

‘Well, the box is lovely, Arthur. Is it really a gift? How sweet of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a sweet. I’ll have it now.’

‘Good heavens, Lady Clem!’ Lord Arthur cried, seizing her hand. ‘You must do no such thing. This is a homeopathic medicine, and taking it when you haven’t got heartburn could do you terrible harm. Wait until you have an attack, then take it. The result will astonish you.’

‘I would like to take it now,’ Lady Clementina said, raising the small transparent capsule to the light, with its floating bubble of liquid aconitine. ‘I’m sure it tastes delicious. The truth is, although I detest doctors, I adore medicines. Still, I’ll save it for my next attack.’

‘And when will that happen?’ Lord Arthur asked eagerly.

For many years Dorian Gray remained unable to shake off the spell of this book. Perhaps it would be truer to say that he made no effort to escape it. He obtained from Paris fully nine large-paper copies of the first edition and ordered bindings in a variety of colours, to answer to his different moods and the shifting whims of a nature that sometimes seemed almost wholly beyond his command. Its hero, the extraordinary young Parisian whose character united the scientific and the romantic in so curious a fashion, came to seem a prophetic image of himself. Indeed, he felt that the entire volume told the tale of his own existence before he had actually lived it.

In one respect his fortune surpassed that of the novel’s fantastical hero. He never experienced—nor, in truth, ever had reason to experience—the rather grotesque terror of looking-glasses, polished metals, and motionless water that seized the young Parisian so early, following the abrupt decline of a beauty that had apparently once been astonishing. With a delight almost cruel—and cruelty perhaps enters into nearly every delight, as it certainly enters every pleasure—he would read the later chapters, with their genuinely tragic, though somewhat exaggerated, depiction of the grief and hopelessness of a man who had lost in himself what he prized above all else in other people and in the world.

For the marvellous beauty that had enchanted Basil Hallward, and so many besides, appeared never to desert him. Even people who had heard the worst reports of him—and strange accounts of his way of living occasionally stole through London and furnished gossip for the clubs—found themselves unable, on seeing him, to credit anything shameful. He always appeared like someone whom the world had left unstained. Men engaged in coarse talk fell quiet when Dorian Gray came into the room. The purity of his countenance seemed to reproach them. Simply by being there, he appeared to remind them of the innocence they had themselves defiled. They wondered that anyone so graceful and delightful could have avoided the taint of an era at once sensual and sordid.

Frequently, after coming home from one of the long, unexplained absences that prompted such curious speculation among his friends, or those who imagined themselves his friends, he would steal up to the locked chamber. Using the key he now always carried, he would let himself in and stand with a looking-glass before the portrait Basil Hallward had made of him. His eyes would move from the wicked, ageing countenance upon the canvas to the lovely, youthful face that smiled in laughter back at him from the shining glass.

No message of sympathy had gone to Ireland. The offender had paid for this omission, for when poor Lady Elliot herself died, Kellynch received no letter of condolence. There was therefore ample cause to fear that the Dalrymples regarded the family tie as ended. The problem was how to repair this troubling breach and regain recognition as cousins; nor did Lady Russell or Mr. Elliot, though considering it more reasonably, dismiss the matter as insignificant. ‘Family relationships were always worth maintaining, and good society always worth cultivating. Lady Dalrymple had rented a house in Laura Place for three months and intended to live handsomely. She had visited Bath the previous year, and Lady Russell had heard her described as a delightful woman. It would be most desirable to restore the connection, provided the Elliots need sacrifice nothing of proper dignity.’

Sir Walter, nevertheless, insisted upon his own method, and eventually addressed his right honourable cousin in a very elaborate letter, overflowing with explanations, apologies, and appeals. Neither Mr. Elliot nor Lady Russell admired its composition, but it achieved everything required: three hastily scribbled lines from the Dowager Viscountess. ‘She felt greatly honoured and would be happy to make their acquaintance.’ The labour was finished; its rewards now followed. Visits were paid in Laura Place; the calling cards of the Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret could be displayed in the most conspicuous positions; and everyone heard of ‘Our cousins in Laura Place’ and ‘Our cousin Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret.’

Anne felt ashamed. Even had Lady Dalrymple and her daughter proved thoroughly agreeable, the commotion surrounding them would still have embarrassed her; but they possessed no distinction whatever. Neither manners, accomplishments, nor intelligence set them above others. Lady Dalrymple owed her reputation as ‘a charming woman’ to having a smile and a courteous reply for everyone. Miss Carteret had even less to offer in conversation and was so unattractive and ungainly that, without her ancestry, she would never have been endured in Camden Place.

Lady Russell admitted that she had looked for something better, yet maintained that ‘the acquaintance was worth possessing.’ When Anne ventured to give Mr. Elliot her own assessment, he conceded that they were unremarkable in themselves. Still, he argued, they had value as family connections, as good company, and as people who would gather good company about them. Anne smiled before replying:

‘To my mind, Mr. Elliot, good company means intelligent, well-informed people with plenty to say. That is what I understand by good company.’
